info.name: Kindlast
info.description:
The Kindlast HTTP surface, against the local compose stack (deploy/compose.yaml).

The collection is committed and reviewed alongside the code it describes, so it grows with the build order rather than drifting in one person's workspace.

**Two halves, with different futures.** The `auth` folder describes endpoints Zitadel serves and `web` redirects to. Those will never appear in a proto file, so this collection stays their source of truth. The `Core API v1` folder describes the proto surface, and once buf emits OpenAPI (design doc §23.2) those requests should be generated rather than hand-written, or the two will disagree.

**Requests marked NOT YET IMPLEMENTED** are here on purpose. They document the contract that the issue named in each description will deliver, so the collection tracks the plan rather than only the past.

No secrets live in this file. The client secret is generated by the seed job and belongs in a Postman environment or a vault, never in the repo.

variable.description: Zitadel. Published by compose on KINDLAST_AUTH_PORT, default 8300.
Caddy edge. Published on KINDLAST_EDGE_PORT, default 8000.
The Next.js app, run with `bun run dev`.
Core API is reached through web, deliberately. It binds no published port (ENT-191), so there is no direct URL to put here.

The web OIDC client, created by the seed job. Read it with:

docker run --rm -v kindlast_zitadel-machinekey:/k alpine cat /k/web-client.json
Seed-generated. Keep it in an environment, never in this file.
Set by the token request's test script.

item.name: Auth (Zitadel)
item.description: Consumed through discovery, never by hard-coded path (§18.2), so a self-hoster can point at their own provider. Every URL below is taken from the discovery document rather than assumed.

// Store the endpoints so later requests use the advertised paths

request.description:
The signing keys core-api verifies against, locally and cached, rather than introspecting per request (§1.4).

**This is `{"keys": []}` on a freshly seeded stack.** Zitadel generates a signing key lazily, on the first token it issues, so an empty set is correct rather than broken. It matters for ENT-195: a JWKS cache populated at boot would cache nothing and then reject every token, which is exactly why the acceptance criterion is that an unknown `kid` triggers a refetch.

exec: // Deliberately not asserting a non-empty set: see the description.
console.log('JWKS is empty, which is expected until the first token is issued.');

item.name: Token, client credentials (NO CLIENT YET, ENT-195)

request.description:
A machine token, for exercising the API without a browser.

**This does not work yet, and not because of a misconfiguration.** The seed job creates one OIDC client, `web`, with the authorization-code and refresh grants only. Giving a confidential browser client the client-credentials grant would be wrong, so the machine clients of §1.3 (`internal:ingest`, `internal:intelligence`, `internal:act-on-behalf`) are a separate thing that ENT-195 adds. The request is kept here as the shape that will work once they exist.

The **user** flow is authorization code with PKCE and cannot be driven from Postman end to end, because it involves a login form and a redirect back to web. Use a browser for that.

exec: // Not an assertion failure: no client-credentials client exists
// yet (ENT-195). Asserting here would make a green stack look
// broken every time somebody runs the folder.
console.log('No client-credentials client yet. Expected until ENT-195; see the request description.');

request.description: The IdP's view of the subject. Note that core-api does not call this per request: it verifies the token locally (§1.4), so auth being down does not take the API down with it.

Revocation reaches the refresh token. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire, which is why sign-out also adds the `jti` to a Redis deny-list (§1.7). Without that second step, sign-out looks like it works and does not, for up to ten minutes.

item.name: web (OAuth client)
item.description:
Browser-facing redirect endpoints on the Next.js app, not `/api/v1`. They are listed for completeness: most cannot be exercised from Postman, because they end in a redirect to a login form.

NOT YET IMPLEMENTED: ENT-197.

request.description:
Builds the authorization URL with a PKCE verifier and state, then 302s. `?idp=google` adds an `idp_hint`.

Follow redirects off to see the 302 rather than the login page.
**POST with a CSRF token, never GET.** A GET logout can be triggered by a prefetch or an image tag, which signs the user out without them acting. ENT-197 asserts a GET is rejected.

item.name: Core API v1
item.description:
The proto surface, reached through web rather than directly: core-api binds no published port, so there is no host to point at (ENT-191).

Once buf emits OpenAPI (§23.2), these requests should be generated from it rather than maintained here by hand.

header.description: The active organisation travels per request rather than in the token, so switching organisation needs no re-minting (§20.1).

request.description:
The console bootstrap call: user, memberships with roles, active organisation, plan.

On a subject it has never seen it provisions a personal organisation and an owner membership in one transaction, idempotent on the `sub` claim. Required scope: `openid`, declared on the proto method.

Ordering matters and is easy to get wrong: this must run **before** the first `/api/v1/me`. Get it backwards and every invited user ends up owning a personal organisation they never asked for, alongside the one they were invited to.
